chunks.text: The arjuna tree (Terminalia arjuna) belongs to the family Combretaceae (order Myrtales). It is found across the Indian subcontinent, typically growing along riverbanks or near dry riverbeds, in states including Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal and Odisha, as well as in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and around Karachi in Pakistan; it has also been introduced to Malaysia, Indonesia and Kenya. The tree grows 20-25 m tall with a distinctive smooth, pale, buttressed trunk and a wide canopy of drooping branches. Its leaves are oblong and conical, green above and brown below, and it bears pale yellow flowers between March and June, followed by distinctive fibrous, woody, five-winged fruits about 2.5-5 cm long that mature from September to November. Ecologically, arjuna is considered a keystone species in the riparian (riverside) forests of southern India: it provides nesting habitat for Malabar giant squirrels and the endangered white-rumped vulture, its dead wood supports termite colonies that in turn feed sloth bears, and its leaves are the food plant of Antheraea paphia moths, whose cocoons are the source of commercially important tassar silk.

chunks.text: Arjuna bark is one of the best-known cardiac remedies in Ayurvedic medicine, with the physician Vagbhata recording its use for heart disease roughly 1,200 years ago; it remains in wide use today, including as an over-the-counter supplement marketed for heart health. Its bark contains tannins, triterpenoid saponins such as arjunic and arjunolic acid, flavonoids, gallic acid, ellagic acid, oligomeric proanthocyanidins and phytosterols. Modern clinical research, including randomised trials in patients with chronic stable angina and congestive heart failure, has examined aqueous bark extract for cardiotonic effects such as improved cardiac function; laboratory studies suggest arjunolic acid may help reduce cardiac fibrosis by inhibiting TGF-beta signalling, though as with any bark-derived supplement, its use should be understood as traditional/complementary rather than a substitute for medical treatment of heart conditions.
